title: Sheila Chepkirui takes back New York’s marathon title as seven seconds divide the podium
subtitle: The Kenyan wins for the second time in three years, while Jess McClain passes defending champion Hellen Obiri to secure an American podium breakthrough.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui reclaimed the New York City Marathon title on 1 November, winning the women’s open race in 2:24:36 as a close contest for the remaining podium places continued behind her.

American Jess McClain finished six seconds later in 2:24:42, overtaking defending champion Hellen Obiri in the closing metres. Obiri, also from Kenya, took third in 2:24:43. Seven seconds separated the three women after 42.195 kilometres.

For Chepkirui, the result was a second New York victory in three years. For McClain, it was her highest finish at a World Marathon Major and the first American women’s open-division podium in New York since Shalane Flanagan finished third in 2018, according to organiser New York Road Runners.
Chepkirui’s own account emphasised the judgment required to beat a rival she knew well. “I had to be patient because I knew Hellen was really strong,” she said, according to AFP.

Reuters reported that Chepkirui was alone when she crossed the line. Behind her, McClain’s late move changed the order of the podium. The narrow margins explain why the finish demanded attention beyond identifying the winner: second and third remained in contention until the final metres.

Obiri’s presence gave the contest particular weight. A year earlier, she had won New York in 2:19:51, taking almost three minutes off the longstanding course record. Chepkirui finished third that day in 2:20:24, behind Sharon Lokedi, as Kenyan women swept the podium.

This year’s winning time was slower, but the finishing order was reversed. That is a useful distinction in distance running: winning a race and setting its fastest time are different achievements. Sunday belonged to Chepkirui’s ability to finish ahead of the women racing beside her.
A season built on close finishes

The victory also extended a successful year for Chepkirui. On 8 March she retained her Nagoya Women’s Marathon title in Japan in 2:21:54. World Athletics reported that she broke clear late from Sayaka Sato, who finished only two seconds behind.

Nagoya and New York were different races, but both ended with Chepkirui converting a close contest into a win. Her November result was therefore more than a return to the site of her 2024 success; it added another title to a season already containing a major women-only marathon victory.

McClain’s runner-up finish supplied a different measure of progress. The organiser described it as her best placing at the sport’s major marathons. Her achievement stands alongside Chepkirui’s rather than explaining it away: one woman regained a title, another reached a new level, and the defending champion remained within seconds of both.
The right to race was contested, too

This year’s marathon marked 50 years of the route through New York’s five boroughs. The anniversary also offers a reason to remember that women’s place in the event was shaped by organised resistance.

In its history of Nina Kuscsik, New York Road Runners recounts how she and five other women sat down at the start of the 1972 marathon to protest the separate start imposed on them. They then got up and raced. Kuscsik won, and returned to defend her title the following year.

Her contribution extended beyond those victories. She lobbied the Amateur Athletic Union to widen women’s access to longer distances and worked with others to bring the women’s marathon into the Olympics, where it finally appeared in 1984.

That history should not turn today’s athletes into symbols at the expense of their performances. Chepkirui deserves to be understood through her decisions and results; McClain through a breakthrough earned at the finish; Obiri through the standard she has set and the challenge she continued to pose.

The connection between the generations is concrete. Earlier runners challenged who was allowed to compete on equal terms. On Sunday, the women at the front gave New York a race whose outcome remained uncertain almost to the line. Their achievement merits the same close attention to skill, tactics and rivalry that makes any great sporting contest worth watching.
